name: Office Trust Records (Trusted Documents)
purpose: Remembers a user's decision to trust a document that triggered a security warning, such as a Protected View or macro warning, so Office does not re-prompt the next time the same file is opened.
key_fields: Value name - full path of the trusted document
Value data - a binary structure encoding the time the document was trusted plus which trust grant was applied (e.g. enabling active content/macros vs. exiting Protected View)
Trust type flags - distinguish a plain trust decision from one that also enabled macro/active-content execution
normal_baseline: A small number of trusted entries corresponding to internal templates, forms, or macro-enabled workbooks the user knowingly and repeatedly uses, trusted once and then opened without further warnings.
anomalies: A macro-enabled document trusted immediately before other compromise indicators, especially one received as an email attachment or downloaded from an external/unexpected sender

A trust decision timestamp only seconds after the document's creation or download time, consistent with a user immediately enabling content on an unfamiliar file rather than a document they habitually use
A trusted document path under Temp, Downloads, or an email-attachment cache directory rather than a normal working location
Multiple documents from the same unfamiliar source or naming pattern trusted in quick succession, suggesting a mass-mailed macro campaign
anti_forensic_notes: A TrustRecords entry is only created after the user actively grants trust - a document opened and then closed without enabling content (or blocked by Protected View and never trusted) leaves no entry here even though it may appear elsewhere (File MRU, Reading Locations). Because trust is granted per full file path, renaming or moving a previously-trusted malicious document forces a fresh trust decision and therefore a fresh, checkable record.
interpretation: This key exists specifically to avoid re-prompting the user, so its presence is direct evidence of an affirmative user action to bypass a security warning, not merely that the file was opened. The stored data includes both the time trust was granted and which specific permission was extended, which for a macro-enabled document is typically the single most important pivot point in reconstructing a phishing-to-execution chain.
